# Problem 1

## Data import and cleaning

```{r}
homicide_df =
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv")

dim(homicide_df)
```
```{r}
homicide_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/homicide-data.csv",
    na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, state, sep = ", "),
    resolved = if_else(disposition == "Closed by arrest", 1, 0),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c(
      "Dallas, TX",
      "Phoenix, AZ",
      "Kansas City, MO",
      "Tulsa, AL"
    ),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    victim_sex = factor(victim_sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    victim_race = factor(victim_race, levels = c("White", "Black"))
  )
```

After data cleaning, the dataset contains
`r nrow(homicide_df)` homicide records across
`r n_distinct(homicide_df$city_state)` cities.
Among these records,
`r scales::percent(mean(homicide_df$resolved, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.1)`
were resolved through arrest. The analysis is restricted
to White and Black victims, with female victims serving
as the reference group for the subsequent logistic
regression analysis.

## Logistic regression for Baltimore

We first fit a logistic regression model for Baltimore, MD,
using homicide resolution as the binary outcome and victim
age, sex, and race as predictors. The model estimates the
association between victim sex and homicide resolution,
adjusting for victim age and race.

```{r}
baltimore_df =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD")

baltimore_fit =
  glm(
    resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
    data = baltimore_df,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
  )
```

```{r}
#extract the OR and 95% CI
baltimore_results =
  baltimore_fit |>
  broom::tidy(
    conf.int = TRUE,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

baltimore_results |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Adjusted OR",
      "95% CI Lower",
      "95% CI Upper"
    )
  )
```
In Baltimore, the adjusted odds ratio for homicide
resolution comparing male victims to female victims is
`r round(baltimore_results$estimate, 3)`
(95% CI:
`r round(baltimore_results$conf.low, 3)` to
`r round(baltimore_results$conf.high, 3)`).
After adjusting for victim age and race, homicides
involving male victims have approximately
`r round((1 - baltimore_results$estimate) * 100, 1)`%
lower odds of resolution than those involving female
victims. The association is statistically significant
because the 95% confidence interval does not include 1.


## Logistic regression across cities

We extend the Baltimore analysis to all cities in the
cleaned dataset by fitting separate logistic regression
models for each city. Each model estimates the adjusted
odds ratio for homicide resolution comparing male victims
to female victims, controlling for victim age and race.

```{r}
city_results =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(data = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    model = map(
      data,
      \(df) glm(
        resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
        data = df,
        family = binomial(link = "logit")
      )
    ),
    results = map(
      model,
      \(fit) broom::tidy(
        fit,
        conf.int = TRUE,
        conf.level = 0.95,
        exponentiate = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  select(city_state, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(city_state, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) |>
  arrange(estimate)
```

```{r}
dim(city_results)

city_results |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
## Visualization of adjusted odds ratios

To compare the association between victim sex and homicide
resolution across cities, we create a forest plot displaying
the adjusted odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals.
Cities are ordered by their estimated odds ratios, and a
reference line at OR = 1 indicates equal adjusted odds of
resolution for male and female victims.


```{r, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 12}
city_results |>
  mutate(
    city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, estimate),
    significance = case_when(
      conf.high < 1 ~ "Significantly lower",
      conf.low > 1 ~ "Significantly higher",
      TRUE ~ "Not statistically significant"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = estimate,
      y = city_state,
      color = significance
    )
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Significantly lower" = "steelblue",
      "Significantly higher" = "firebrick",
      "Not statistically significant" = "gray60"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Odds Ratios for Homicide Resolution",
    subtitle = "Male versus female victims, adjusting for age and race",
    x = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)",
    y = "City",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: The Washington Post"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r}
#Final statistic 
city_summary =
  city_results |>
  summarize(
    n_cities = n(),
    n_lower_or = sum(estimate < 1),
    n_higher_or = sum(estimate > 1),
    n_significant_lower = sum(conf.high < 1),
    n_significant_higher = sum(conf.low > 1),
    n_not_significant = sum(conf.low <= 1 & conf.high >= 1)
  )

city_summary |>
  knitr::kable()
```
The forest plot shows that `r city_summary$n_lower_or` of
the `r city_summary$n_cities` cities
(`r round(city_summary$n_lower_or / city_summary$n_cities * 100, 1)`%)
have estimated adjusted odds ratios below 1, suggesting
lower odds of homicide resolution for male victims after
adjusting for age and race.

Among all cities, `r city_summary$n_significant_lower`
have 95% confidence intervals entirely below 1, while
`r city_summary$n_significant_higher` have confidence
intervals entirely above 1. The remaining
`r city_summary$n_not_significant` cities have confidence
intervals that include 1.

New York has the lowest estimated adjusted odds ratio
(`r round(min(city_results$estimate), 3)`), while
Albuquerque has the highest
(`r round(max(city_results$estimate), 3)`).
The widths of the confidence intervals vary across cities,
indicating differences in the precision of the estimates.

Overall, homicides involving male victims tend to have
lower adjusted odds of resolution than those involving
female victims, although the magnitude and statistical
significance of this association vary across cities.


#Problem 2

```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(p8105.datasets)

```

## Data import and preparation

```{r}
data("weather_df")

weather_df =
  weather_df |>
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp) |>
  drop_na()

weather_df |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable()
```
```{r}
dim(weather_df)

summary(weather_df)
```
## Original linear regression model

We first fit a linear regression model using the original
weather dataset to obtain reference estimates for the
subsequent bootstrap analysis.

```{r}
weather_fit =
  lm(
    tmax ~ tmin + prcp,
    data = weather_df
  )

weather_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```
```{r}
original_r_squared =
  weather_fit |>
  broom::glance() |>
  pull(r.squared)

original_ratio =
  weather_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  ) |>
  mutate(beta_ratio = tmin / prcp) |>
  pull(beta_ratio)

tibble(
  r_squared = original_r_squared,
  beta_ratio = original_ratio
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```
```{r}
#create bootstrap result
boot_sample = function(df) {
  slice_sample(
    df,
    n = nrow(df),
    replace = TRUE
  )
}

boot_sample = function(df) {
  slice_sample(
    df,
    n = nrow(df),
    replace = TRUE
  )
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

bootstrap_results =
  tibble(bootstrap_id = 1:5000) |>
  mutate(
    boot_sample = map(
      bootstrap_id,
      \(i) boot_sample(weather_df)
    ),
    model = map(
      boot_sample,
      \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)
    ),
    r_squared = map_dbl(
      model,
      \(fit) broom::glance(fit) |> pull(r.squared)
    ),
    coefficients = map(
      model,
      \(fit) broom::tidy(fit)
    )
  ) |>
  select(bootstrap_id, r_squared, coefficients) |>
  unnest(coefficients) |>
  select(bootstrap_id, r_squared, term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  ) |>
  mutate(beta_ratio = tmin / prcp) |>
  select(bootstrap_id, r_squared, beta_ratio)

dim(bootstrap_results)

bootstrap_results |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```
```{r}
bootstrap_results |>
  summarize(
    invalid_r_squared = sum(!is.finite(r_squared)),
    invalid_beta_ratio = sum(!is.finite(beta_ratio))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
## Bootstrap distributions

We visualize the bootstrap distributions of R-squared
and the coefficient ratio to examine their shapes,
centers, and variability. The dashed vertical lines
represent the estimates obtained from the original
dataset.

```{r}
bootstrap_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = r_squared)) +
  geom_density(
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "steelblue4",
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = original_r_squared,
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distribution of R-squared",
    subtitle = "Based on 5,000 bootstrap samples",
    x = "R-squared",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
bootstrap_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = beta_ratio)) +
  geom_density(
    fill = "seagreen3",
    color = "seagreen4",
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = original_ratio,
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distribution of the Coefficient Ratio",
    subtitle = "Based on 5,000 bootstrap samples",
    x = expression(hat(beta)[1] / hat(beta)[2]),
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
## Bootstrap confidence intervals

We construct 95% percentile-based bootstrap confidence
intervals using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the
bootstrap distributions for both statistics.

```{r}
bootstrap_ci =
  bootstrap_results |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(r_squared, beta_ratio),
    names_to = "statistic",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  group_by(statistic) |>
  summarize(
    bootstrap_mean = mean(estimate),
    bootstrap_se = sd(estimate),
    conf.low = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    conf.high = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bootstrap_ci |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c(
      "Statistic",
      "Bootstrap Mean",
      "Bootstrap SE",
      "95% CI Lower",
      "95% CI Upper"
    ),
    caption = "95% percentile-based bootstrap confidence intervals"
  )
```
```{r}
r_squared_ci =
  bootstrap_ci |>
  filter(statistic == "r_squared")

beta_ratio_ci =
  bootstrap_ci |>
  filter(statistic == "beta_ratio")
```

## Final interpretation

Based on `r nrow(bootstrap_results)` bootstrap samples,
the bootstrap distribution of R-squared is tightly
concentrated around its original estimate of
`r round(original_r_squared, 4)`, with a bootstrap mean
of `r round(r_squared_ci$bootstrap_mean, 4)` and a
standard error of `r round(r_squared_ci$bootstrap_se, 4)`.
The 95% bootstrap confidence interval is
(`r round(r_squared_ci$conf.low, 4)`,
`r round(r_squared_ci$conf.high, 4)`).
The narrow confidence interval suggests that the
estimated proportion of variation in maximum temperature
explained by the model is relatively stable across
bootstrap samples.

The bootstrap distribution of the coefficient ratio
is unimodal and negatively skewed, with a longer tail
toward more negative values. The original estimate is
`r round(original_ratio, 4)`, while the bootstrap mean
is `r round(beta_ratio_ci$bootstrap_mean, 4)`.
The 95% bootstrap confidence interval is
(`r round(beta_ratio_ci$conf.low, 4)`,
`r round(beta_ratio_ci$conf.high, 4)`).
The asymmetric distribution illustrates the usefulness
of percentile-based bootstrap confidence intervals
when a normal approximation may be inappropriate.

Overall, the regression model explains a large
proportion of the observed variation in maximum
temperature. Bootstrap resampling provides an empirical
approach to quantifying uncertainty in both R-squared
and the ratio of regression coefficients without
requiring a normal sampling distribution.



# Problem 3

## Data import and cleaning

We investigate factors associated with infant birthweight
using multiple linear regression and compare the predictive
performance of three regression models using cross-validation.

```{r}
birthweight_df =
  read_csv("data/birthweight.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    babysex = factor(
      babysex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    frace = factor(
      frace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9),
      labels = c(
        "White", "Black", "Asian",
        "Puerto Rican", "Other", "Unknown"
      )
    ),
    mrace = factor(
      mrace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8),
      labels = c(
        "White", "Black", "Asian",
        "Puerto Rican", "Other"
      )
    ),
    malform = factor(
      malform,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Absent", "Present")
    )
  )

dim(birthweight_df)

glimpse(birthweight_df)
```
```{r}
missing_summary =
  birthweight_df |>
  summarize(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "n_missing"
  )

missing_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing observations"),
    caption = "Missing data summary"
  )

sum(!complete.cases(birthweight_df))
```
After data cleaning, the dataset contains
`r nrow(birthweight_df)` observations and
`r ncol(birthweight_df)` variables.
Infant sex, maternal race, paternal race, and the
presence of malformations were converted to categorical
variables. The dataset contains
`r sum(is.na(birthweight_df))` missing values and
`r sum(!complete.cases(birthweight_df))` incomplete
observations. Therefore, all observations can be retained
for the subsequent regression analysis.


## Proposed regression model

A hypothesis-driven approach was used to select predictors
for the proposed birthweight regression model. Infant sex,
head circumference, birth length, and gestational age were
included to account for infant size and development.
Maternal smoking, pre-pregnancy BMI, pregnancy weight gain,
maternal age, and maternal race were included to account
for maternal behavioral, physiological, and demographic
characteristics.

A multiple linear regression model was fitted using
birthweight as the continuous outcome and the selected
predictors as main effects.

```{r}
birthweight_fit =
  lm(
    bwt ~ babysex + bhead + blength + gaweeks +
      smoken + ppbmi + wtgain + momage + mrace,
    data = birthweight_df
  )

birthweight_fit |>
  broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Estimated coefficients for the proposed model"
  )
```
```{r}
birthweight_fit |>
  broom::glance() |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, nobs) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c(
      "R-squared",
      "Adjusted R-squared",
      "Residual standard error",
      "Observations"
    ),
    caption = "Summary of proposed regression model"
  )
```
## Model diagnostics

```{r}
birthweight_diagnostics =
  birthweight_df |>
  modelr::add_predictions(birthweight_fit) |>
  modelr::add_residuals(birthweight_fit)

birthweight_diagnostics |>
  select(bwt, pred, resid) |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
birthweight_diagnostics |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.25,
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "darkorange"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals versus Fitted Values",
    subtitle = "Diagnostic plot for the proposed birthweight model",
    x = "Fitted birthweight (grams)",
    y = "Residuals (grams)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The residuals are generally centered around zero for
most fitted birthweights, suggesting that the proposed
linear regression model provides a reasonable fit for
the majority of observations. However, the smoothing
curve deviates substantially from zero at lower fitted
values, indicating potential nonlinearity and systematic
underprediction in this region. Several large residuals
and negative fitted birthweights are also observed.
The varying spread of residuals suggests potential
heteroscedasticity. These findings indicate that the
model has limitations, particularly for infants with
extreme fitted birthweights.

## Alternative regression models

To evaluate the predictive performance of the proposed
model, two alternative regression models were fitted.
The first includes birth length and gestational age
as main effects, while the second includes head
circumference, birth length, infant sex, and all
possible interactions among these three predictors.

```{r}
length_age_fit =
  lm(
    bwt ~ blength + gaweeks,
    data = birthweight_df
  )

interaction_fit =
  lm(
    bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex,
    data = birthweight_df
  )
```

```{r}
model_comparison =
  tibble(
    model = c(
      "Proposed model",
      "Length and gestational age",
      "Full interaction model"
    ),
    fit = list(
      birthweight_fit,
      length_age_fit,
      interaction_fit
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model_summary = map(fit, broom::glance)
  ) |>
  select(-fit) |>
  unnest(model_summary) |>
  select(model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma)

model_comparison |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c(
      "Model",
      "R-squared",
      "Adjusted R-squared",
      "Residual standard error"
    ),
    caption = "Comparison of regression model fit"
  )
```
```{r}
set.seed(123)

cv_df =
  birthweight_df |>
  modelr::crossv_mc(100, test = 0.2) |>
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble),
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )

cv_df
```
```{r}
cv_df =
  cv_df |>
  mutate(
    proposed_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(formula(birthweight_fit), data = df)
    ),
    length_age_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(formula(length_age_fit), data = df)
    ),
    interaction_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(formula(interaction_fit), data = df)
    )
  )

cv_df
```
#I want a better RMSE better predictive performance
```{r}
cv_df =
  cv_df |>
  mutate(
    rmse_proposed = map2_dbl(
      proposed_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    ),
    rmse_length_age = map2_dbl(
      length_age_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    ),
    rmse_interaction = map2_dbl(
      interaction_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    )
  )

cv_df |>
  select(.id, starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
```{r}
cv_summary =
  cv_df |>
  select(starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(
      model,
      rmse_proposed = "Proposed model",
      rmse_length_age = "Length and gestational age",
      rmse_interaction = "Full interaction model"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
    median_rmse = median(rmse),
    sd_rmse = sd(rmse),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(mean_rmse)

cv_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Model",
      "Mean RMSE",
      "Median RMSE",
      "SD of RMSE"
    ),
    caption = "Comparison of cross-validated prediction errors"
  )
```
## Comparison of cross-validated prediction errors

```{r}
cv_plot_df =
  cv_df |>
  select(.id, starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  pivot_longer(

```


```{r}
proposed_cv =
  cv_summary |>
  filter(model == "Proposed model")

interaction_cv =
  cv_summary |>
  filter(model == "Full interaction model")

length_age_cv =
  cv_summary |>
  filter(model == "Length and gestational age")

improvement_simple =
  (length_age_cv$mean_rmse -
     proposed_cv$mean_rmse) /
  length_age_cv$mean_rmse

improvement_interaction =
  (interaction_cv$mean_rmse -
     proposed_cv$mean_rmse) /
  interaction_cv$mean_rmse
```


## Final interpretation

The proposed regression model explains
`r scales::percent(broom::glance(birthweight_fit)$r.squared, accuracy = 0.1)`
of the observed variation in birthweight. The residuals
are generally centered around zero for the majority of
observations. However, the residual plot shows curvature
at lower fitted values and several large residuals,
suggesting that the model may not adequately capture
birthweight variation among some observations.

Based on `r nrow(cv_df)` Monte Carlo cross-validation
repetitions, the proposed model achieves the lowest
mean RMSE of
`r round(proposed_cv$mean_rmse, 2)` grams,
compared with
`r round(interaction_cv$mean_rmse, 2)` grams for the
full interaction model and
`r round(length_age_cv$mean_rmse, 2)` grams for the
length and gestational age model.

The proposed model reduces mean prediction error by
`r scales::percent(improvement_simple, accuracy = 0.1)`
relative to the length and gestational age model and
`r scales::percent(improvement_interaction, accuracy = 0.1)`
relative to the full interaction model.

The violin plot also shows that the proposed model
has lower prediction errors and less variability
across repeated training and testing splits.

Overall, the proposed model provides the best predictive
performance among the three candidate models. Although
the residual diagnostics suggest some limitations,
the cross-validation results support selecting the
proposed model for birthweight prediction.
